title: The special senses
note: Each special sense turns one kind of stimulus into receptor potentials: chemicals for taste and smell, fluid waves bending hair cells for hearing and balance, and light absorbed by photopigments for vision. Smell is the only sense that reaches the cortex without first relaying in the thalamus.

read.title: How the ear sorts pitch
text: Sound reaches the ear as pressure waves in air. They vibrate the tympanic membrane, and three tiny bones, the malleus, incus, and stapes, pass the motion inward. Because the eardrum is much larger than the oval window where the stapes presses, the force is concentrated, which helps drive vibrations into the fluid of the cochlea.

Inside the coiled cochlea, the pressure waves travel through fluid and flex the basilar membrane. On this membrane sits the organ of Corti, lined with hair cells. When the membrane moves, the stereocilia on the hair cells bend against the overlying tectorial membrane. Bending opens ion channels and the hair cell signals to sensory neurons of the vestibulocochlear nerve.

The basilar membrane is not uniform. Near its base, close to the oval window, it is narrow and stiff and vibrates most for high frequencies. Toward the apex it is wider and more flexible and responds best to low frequencies. A given pitch therefore makes one region vibrate most, and the brain reads pitch from which hair cells are firing.
The same hair-cell trick serves balance. In the utricle and saccule and in the semicircular canals, head movement shifts gel or fluid and bends stereocilia.

q.q: Which part of the basilar membrane responds most to high pitches?
o: The base, near the oval window
